❯ Write a 900-word story about a lighthouse keeper, directly in your reply, no tools.

● The lighthouse on Carrow Point had stood for a hundred and twelve years, and for the last thirty of them Elias
  Wren had kept its lamp. He climbed the iron stairs every evening at dusk, one hundred and forty-seven steps,
  and every morning he climbed down again. In between, he wound the clockwork, trimmed the wick, polished the
  great lens until the glass held no fingerprints, and wrote the weather in a ledger that nobody read.

  The ledger was the only thing he had kept from his father, who had kept the light before him. The first page
  was filled with a careful copper-plate hand that recorded wind from the northwest, fog in the early hours, a
  schooner lost off the eastern reef in the autumn of 1931. Elias had continued the record in his own cramped
  handwriting, and sometimes he turned back through the pages in the long winter nights just to hear the rhythm
  of the entries, the small daily facts that added up to a life.

  Most of the village had moved inland decades ago. The fishing fleet had dwindled to three boats, and the
  cannery was a shell of rusted tin with gulls nesting in its rafters. Elias saw the mail boat twice a month and
  the supply truck once a week, and that was enough. He had never been good at company. He was good at weather,
  at timing the tides, at knowing that the light needed to turn exactly so many times a minute or the ships out
  past the shoals would lose their bearings.

  In March, a letter came on the mail boat. The envelope was thick and cream-colored, addressed in an unfamiliar
  script. Elias read it standing at the bottom of the tower, the wind pushing at his coat. It was from the
  Northern Lights Authority. The station was to be automated by the end of the year. A satellite-linked beacon
  would replace the lens, the clockwork, and the man. The letter thanked him for his thirty years of service and
  offered a pension, a modest one, and a small cottage in the town of Harrow, forty miles inland.

  He folded the letter and put it in his pocket. He did not feel anger, exactly. He had seen the ships change
  from sail to steam to diesel, and he had watched the radio masts climb along the coast like a slow tide of
  steel. Automation was simply the next thing. But he felt something heavier, a kind of weight settling into his
  chest, and it took him most of the evening to name it. It was grief, though not for the light. It was grief
  for the quiet, for the hours of solitude that had made him feel like part of something enormous and patient.
